text: This is like a lottery winner who takes his winnings and buys more lottery tickets. Complete reinvestment in newbuildings over a long period of time will end up with too many tankers chasing too few cargoes. At one point or another, the winnings are going to be given up to someone else. One famous Norwegian owner managed to convert a billion dollar shipping fortune to a billion dollar negative net worth by pursuing this strategy. What To Do? This is a complex strategic question whose response varies from company to company. Paying dividends reduces the scope of the challenge by making shareholders partially responsible for addressing this issue. Paying off cheap debt when other more promising areas of cash disposal are available does not seem an optimal strategy. Investing in new areas depends on what these areas are. They could be an excellent opportunity to diversify holdings, but this depends on the nature of the investment and its risk profile as compared to shipping. In retrospect, this was the best course of action for cash generated during the 1970s tanker boom. Buying existing tankers or a tanker owning company, while certainly a viable alternative, involves paying record high values. Waiting for ship values to fall can be ultimately self-defeating if too many are waiting and watching. With shipping stocks selling substantially above book value, issuing new stock and buying ships at even today's inflated values may not be an unreasonable course of action. While ordering another vessel at today's ship prices may not seem attractive, an order or two, when blended in with a fleet acquired at lower costs, may make sense particularly if employment seems assured. In our opinion, the only dangerous strategy is for the tanker industry to double its bet by taking their winnings and ordering a slew of newbuildings. This strategy would eventually flood the market with excess capacity destroying the present delicate balance between supply and demand, bringing about another tanker recession. This is a situation that owners and charterers would do well to avoid.

text: This past week, the Eleventh Annual Shipping Conference sponsored by the Hellenic-American and the Norwegian-American Chambers of Commerce was held in New York. This relatively low key conference is one of the jewels of the industry. This year's conference on "Shipping without Borders" featured leading luminaries from a cross section of the maritime industry. While impossible to highlight every speaker, the following tidbits are offered to encompass the principal themes of the conference. Although speaking near the end, perhaps the spirit of the conference was best captured by Peter Georgiopoulos , Chairman and President of General Maritime. He showed a slide of Aristotle Onassis standing by his yacht. To Peter, this epitomized the world of shipping when he began his distinguished career. Then the reality of shipping was in the next slide jammed with acronyms of all the organizations, regulations, and laws that shipowners have to contend with. The final slide was of Aristotle wistfully looking into the distance captioned, "What would he do now?" Perspectives on National Identity Leif Hoegh represented the Norwegian shipping community and noted the drift of Norwegian companies away from Norway, not only in terms of domicile, but also in terms of manning and operational management. Acquiring the best people for these tasks transcends national origins far more today than in the past. Moreover management thinking in Norwegian shipping companies is becoming more in tune with financial returns than in acquiring assets flying the Norwegian flag. Norwegian operations are increasingly being conducted in an environment void of borders, but at the same time Norwegian shipping is suffering in this new brave world.

The most recent OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (www.opec.org) listing of world oil inventories shows an uptrend, but does this presage a potential cutback in tanker cargoes if there is a return to "normalcy," given relatively flat oil consumption in Western Europe and OECD Pacific regions and marked increases in North American consumption?
There are two general types of inventory- inventory held by commercial interests and government sponsored Strategic Petroleum Reserves. Commercial inventories are made up of crude oil and oil products, while Strategic Petroleum Reserves (SPRs) are government-controlled and owned inventories of primarily crude oil dedicated to buffer potential interruptions in global oil flows.

text: Inv On Land Inv On the Water Total land inventories have climbed 160 million barrels since 1997 plus another 80 million barrels increase in floating inventory, which of course reflects a greater volume of global oil flows. The overall impact has been a reduction in total inventories from 83 days of consumption to 80 days of consumption since 1997. So What Does This Mean for Tanker Owners? It is true that world oil inventories have increased in the last seven years. However, this situation does not portend a decrease in tanker demand. In fact, the fall in consumption days covered both by commercial inventories and overall worldwide inventories seems to indicate that demand growth has outstripped supply growth. Countries and customers are burning through oil at greater speeds in theory, increasing the cushion that commercial companies and governments require. It becomes thus necessary for these companies to buy up more oil for storage, a requirement that will become incrementally more difficult as tonnage supply is eaten up by China's imminent build-up of a Strategic Petroleum Reserve of its own. Increasing inventories that have lagged the consumption habits of their consumers in fact paint an optimistic picture of tanker demand. The future appears even brighter.

text: Goldman Sachs did a gutsy thing: they stuck their neck out. They have publicly commented that the upper range of their price forecast might spike at $105 per barrel. A similar $100 per barrel forecast was made in the aftermath of the price hikes accompanying the Iranian Revolution in the late 1970s. It didn't happen then, but will it happen now? To be fair, the forecast is not without foundation. The forecast is based on what would happen if there is continued growth in oil demand in the United States and China plus other Asian nations commensurate with the past, coupled with limited potential growth in non-OPEC sources in the near term, and an apparent lack of any significant surplus production capacity within OPEC. With or without supply disruptions, the market will remain tight. The only way to loosen the market is to cut consumption. With Americans still the gas guzzlers of the planet, what will it take for them to cut their gasoline purchases. 10-Year 30-Day The differential between long and short term rates is narrowing only because the Federal Reserve increased overnight Fed rates to 2.75%. Long term rates are relatively unchanged. One reason for the increase in short term rates is to fight inflation by increasing borrowing costs. This is supposed to dampen demand in order to cool off the economy. This contention worked well historically when inflation reflected industrial capacity and labor availability peaking out, causing prices and labor costs to rise. This hardly fits the U.S. economy today. With manufacturing fleeing our shores and industrial activity below capacity, inflation reflects rising energy costs among other factors. Rising energy costs increase food prices, another component in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The CPI is also influenced by higher priced imports from all over the world other than China from a weaker dollar. Cheap goods from China reduce the rise in the CPI. Another reason for the Federal Reserve increasing short term rates is to make dollar deposits by foreigners more attractive in order to strengthen the dollar in relation to other currencies. As the dollar strengthens, the cost of imports from nations other than China, where the yuan and dollar are pegged, falls, thus reducing the rise in the CPI.
Are There Indications of an Economic Slowdown? Not yet: the GDP for the United States strengthened in 2003 and does not show signs of abating (constant dollars show the real rate of change in the GDP). The growth between the fourth quarter of 2003 and the fourth quarter of 2004 was a respectable 3.9%.

Several caveats, or rather constraints are in order. Current refining capacity is operating at high levels of utilization with relatively little spare capacity. With refinery expansion under construction and in the planning stage totaling only a little over 2 million bpd, a rather robust refinery construction program would be necessary to refine incremental demand of 6 million bpd. There is some evidence that U.S. gasoline demand is leveling off. A far greater impact of high oil prices is not a change in driving habits, but a slowing of economic activity. Unfortunately, it is difficult to project a turning point in economic activity until after a turning point begins to occur.

On May 25th, the leaders of Azerbaijan, Georgia, Turkey, and Kazakhstan gathered in Baku along with oil company officials to mark the inauguration of oil flowing in the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline. The $3.2 billion, 42 inch, 1 million bpd capacity pipeline runs 1,090 miles from Baku though Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey to the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan. The pipeline bypasses the congested Bosphorus Strait through which tankers transport oil from the Caspian Pipeline and other Black Sea ports.
The BTC pipeline was developed by an international consortium of 11 partners led by BP as operator with a 30.1% share, the state oil company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR) with a 25% share along with Unocal (8.9%), Statoil 8.71%, TPAO (6.53%), ENI (5%), TotalFinaElf (5%), Itochu (3.4%), INPEX (2.5%), ConocoPhillips (2.5%), and Amerada Hess (2.36%). The pipeline has a design life of 40 years with two pumping stations in Azerbaijan, two in Georgia, and four in Turkey with a flow speed of 2 meters per second (about 4.5 miles per hour). A new terminal was built in Sangachal, Baku, and a new terminal is near completion at Ceyhan, the terminus of the Iraq-Turkey pipeline. The new Ceyhan terminal will have seven new crude oil storage tanks and a jetty that can load two tankers up to 300,000 dwt simultaneously. The BTC pipeline project began with the signing of a Production Sharing Agreement to handle a cluster of oil discoveries offshore Caspian known collectively as the Azeri, Chirag, Gunashli (ACG) oil field. The development of this field needed an outlet to the world market. Although upgrading or building a new pipeline to the Black Sea was considered, the end result of five years of technical and commercial studies was the present route bypassing the Bosphorus Strait and its congestion and environmental concerns. Russia objected to the BTC pipeline as it provided an outlet of Caspian crude that did not rely on the Russian pipeline system. Iran wanted a pipeline running straight from the Caspian Sea to an Iranian export port.

text:
Of all forms of oil, fuel oil is one of the worst pollutants as it has no light ends to evaporate. It is a persistent pollutant that, for the most part, only nature can slowly disperse. The Erika , a Handymax of 36,694 dwt, sank in 1999 and a part of its fuel oil cargo reached the French coast creating a public uproar. Oil companies responded by chartering a greater percentage of cargoes on more modern and generally double hull tankers. The effective reduction in tanker supply by charterer preference for newer tonnage caused an upsurge in rates. A relatively short time later the Prestige , an Aframax of 81,259 dwt, sank in 2002 with part of its fuel oil cargo polluting the coastlines of Spain and Portugal. Oil companies again shifted to newer tonnage, further reducing the availability of suitable tonnage, causing rates to surge again. Tougher standards by charterers were not enough to calm the public outcry. The EU took matters in its own hands and unilaterally banned single hull tankers in European ports from carrying heavy grade oil such as heavy crudes, fuel oil, and bitumen. The ban promulgated in July 2003 became effective in October 2003. The EU also announced that it wanted to accelerate the phase out of single hull tankers calling on European ports as originally scheduled. The unilateral action taken by the EU with regard to hastening the phase out of single hull tankers was eventually adopted, with some modifications, by the IMO when it amended Marpol Regulation 13G. The EU banning of heavy oil cargoes in single hull tankers was incorporated in Marpol Regulation 13H. As of April 2005, single hull tankers above 5,000 dwt are prohibited from carrying heavy grade oils including fuel oils to and from ports of signatory nations.
In addition to the ongoing fleet renewal that is occurring, regulatory changes are clearly impacting the Panamax sector. As show below, the role of single hull Panamax tankers is clearly declining.

text: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) was established in December 1975 as a consequence of the Arab oil embargo of 1973. Its purpose was to have a 700 million barrel reserve of crude oil in the event the United States faced another embargo. The SPR received its first shipment in October 1977 after the salt dome storage facilities in the U.S. Gulf had been set up. text: It took 15 years for the SPR to reach 600 million barrels (1990) and remained near that level until President George W. Bush's election in 2000 when the fill resumed. The current fill rate of between 75,000 and 100,000 barrels per day will shortly cease when the SPR reaches 700 million, the limit set by Congress. However the fill could continue with Congressional approval as the total physical capacity of the SPR is 727 million barrels. Moreover it is possible that Congress could authorize the expansion of SPR capacity to 1 billion barrels, but not in the immediate future. Oil market commentators have been trying to figure out who is going to increase oil production to avert the calamitous economic effects of $100 per barrel oil. About every two weeks or so there is another declaration of soon-to-be increased production that is becoming reminiscent of the boy who cried "Wolf" once too often. Discussing who might increase production ignores the more immediate issue of whose production is slipping. Coupled with continuing oil consumption growth in China and the United States, declines in oil output make step-ups in production by other nations all the more necessary. Let's take OPEC member Indonesia as an example.
Indonesia was one of the first nations to develop its oil industry following earlier developments in the United States and Russia (Black Sea) spearheaded by the Royal Dutch Petroleum and Shell Transport and Trading. Production peaked in 1977 at 1.7 million bpd, then went into a decline until new oil fields were developed. Another peak was reached in 1991 at just under 1.7 million bpd and a decline ensued without the benefit of another oil discovery to 1.1 million bpd in 2004. With strong growth in domestic demand, Indonesia is on the cusp of becoming a net oil importer. Indonesia has recently discussed leaving or downgrading its participation in OPEC to observer membership. U.K. Transitioning to an Oil Importer The days of the U.K. being a net exporter appear again to be numbered. North Sea production of 5.2 million bpd in 2004 is 800,000 bpd off from its peak of 6 million bpd in 1999. Norway has been able to sustain its production, but a decline is just beginning to set in. This year the shortfall in North Sea production will probably exceed 1 million bpd just as the BTC pipeline ramps up to its throughput of 1 million bpd.

Both the volume of inventory and the days of inventory on hand have been in a general decline, reflecting a changing attitude towards inventory from that of an asset to a cost. "Just in Time" operations treat inventory as a cost that should be reduced to an absolute minimum. text: On July 30th, the Senate passed the U.S. Energy Act of 2005 and it is expected to be signed into law by President Bush in New Mexico, home state for Senator Domenici, Senate architect of the energy bill. It has taken four years to pass the Act after a task force headed by Vice President Cheney called for a new approach towards energy, much of which is incorporated in the Act. The proposed legislation was stymied by various lobbyists who opposed portions of the bill and by environmentalists who opposed oil exploration in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR) and in offshore waters now considered off limits. The 1,273 page Act starts out with a long section on how Federal buildings are to reduce their energy consumption by 20% by 2015 through energy conservation, buying energy efficient equipment, and greater use of recovered mineral (e.g. fly ash) in government cement purchases. Each individual state is to report on measures being taken to reduce energy consumption in 2012 by 25% from 1992 levels. The Energy Star program to enhance energy efficiency of home appliances is given a renewed lease on life by the inclusion of washing machines and dishwashers over the next few years. A public education program is to be established to inform the public of the benefits of living with less energy. Public utilities are to reduce energy consumption through promotion of energy conservation and efficiency. The Act is replete with detailed technical requirements for lamps, dehumidifiers and other appliances, transformers, battery chargers, fans, commercial heating and cooling equipment. Government monies are set aside for programs in developing fuel efficient engines for aircraft and tires for motor vehicles; thus ending the first 125 pages of the Act.

text: Hurricane Katrina's effect on New Orleans and surrounding areas has been likened to the 1906 San Francisco earthquake that essentially wiped out an entire city. Like Katrina's impact on New Orleans, much of the resulting damage to San Francisco was collateral in nature. The earthquake shattered buildings, but it also shattered manufactured gas and water pipelines. Fires started by the broken gas mains could not be put out because of the broken water mains. As a result, much of San Francisco burned to the ground. In a similar fashion, Katrina did not do a great deal of damage initially, but after it passed New Orleans, the water continued to rise through breached levees. Katrina's full fury was felt along the Mississippi coastline around Gulfport and Biloxi where a tsunami-like surge 20 or more feet high washed away everything up to one mile inland. As bad as the situation is in New Orleans, it might be worth remembering that a flattened and burned out San Francisco was rebuilt. The economic repercussions are yet to be played out. The economy of this part of the United States is wrecked with hundreds of thousands losing all their possessions (homes, furnishings, automobiles) plus their jobs. But rebuilding can also be a spur to economic activity as was learned in the wake of Hurricane Andrew that left southern Florida in ruin. Economic recovery from World War Two made Europe and Japan greater economic powers than they were before the war. But Katrina has had substantial impacts on the energy market that in turn may have long-lasting effects on the tanker market. Crude oil inventories were down to 321 million barrels as of August 26, off somewhat from the 2005 peak level of 334 million barrels in May of this year, but well above the year-earlier level of 287 million barrels. Of more vital concern are gasoline and gasoil inventories. Gasoline inventories stood at 194 million barrels as of August 26, down from the peak level of 224 million barrels in February of this year and down from 207 million barrels a year earlier. However, with the summer gasoline seasonal peak coming to an end, the nation now faces the winter heating oil seasonal peak with a gasoil inventory of 133 million barrels, the peak level for this year, but up from 125 million barrels same time last year. While the inventory situation doesn't look that bad on the surface, the overall problem extends far beyond inventory levels.

text: Rapidly Increasing Although Brazil has exhibited significant overall economic progress averaging 4.5% since 1981, growth has been marked by fits and starts with contractions occurring regularly followed by spurts of rapid growth. The latest retreat occurred in 2003 when the economy faltered with negative growth of 0.2%, but rapidly recouped in 2004 with growth of 5.1%. These fits and starts in economic growth are reflected in oil consumption. While the oil industry has been liberalized to permit foreign participation in the late 1990s, Petrobras still controls over 95% of the crude oil production. About 80% of Brazil's total production is offshore Rio de Janeiro state in very deep waters of the Campos Basin. The world record for drilling in the deepest waters regularly passes between Petrobras and companies drilling in the Gulf of Mexico. Crude oil from the Campos Basin is an unusual heavy sweet grade. About 1.3-1.4 million bpd of additional production is scheduled to come on stream by 2008. Considering that the gap between consumption and production has narrowed to 0.3 million bpd, it appears that Brazil is rapidly approaching a point of not only self- sufficiency, but also becoming a net exporter. Normally approaching self-sufficiency is bad news for tanker owners. But Brazil is an unusual nation in that its refineries are not geared to process heavy sweet crude. Rather than undergoing extremely costly upgrading of its refineries to handle Campos crude, Brazil has found it to be in its economically expedient to export Campos crude for refining elsewhere and importing oil products. text: OPEC's website (www.opec.org) has a lot of interesting information on its plans to expand crude oil and refinery expansion. If we view high oil prices as the consequence of the supply of oil production and refinery capacity feeling the pinch of 85 million bpd demand, which continues to grow, then this information is invaluable in assessing the future direction of tanker prospects. Crude Production Constraints As we have noted previously in our report "The Fall of Oil Empires" of July 8, 2005, the United States, the United Kingdom, Indonesia, Colombia, and Egypt have falling production. "The Rise of Oil Empires" of July 15, 2005 noted higher production in North and West Africa (a mix of OPEC and non-OPEC producers), Russia, Kazakhstan (BTC pipeline), plus Brazil ("Brazil- Heavy, but Sweet" of December 16, 2005). The net contribution of the rising and falling oil empires is not enough to meet the growing worldwide demand centered in India, China, and the United States (see Tanker Prospects for details). Thus growing world demand means more cargoes from somewhere and that somewhere by default is primarily from the Arabian Gulf OPEC exporters. As seen on the next page, OPEC's production capacity is slated to grow from 32 million barrels per day to 38 million bpd by 2010. Export availability is OPEC production less domestic consumption and perhaps some expansion of spare capacity. In a world of growing demand, export availability could be interpreted as export demand. With the exception of 2006 where export availability declines by 100,000 bpd, the other years exhibit a positive incremental annual gain of 700,000 bpd. While this appears robust, every bit of this incremental supply is going to be needed if world oil demand continues to grow at 2 million bpd. From this viewpoint, we anticipate that tightness in crude oil supply will be with us at least for the next few years, if not longer.

A Major New Trade Emerging? The significant expansion of Middle East refinery capacity along with refinery expansion plans in India and China stand in stark contrast to what is happening in the Western Hemisphere. Yes, there will be refinery creep that expands overall capacity and yes, there is talk about building new refineries (as long as they're not located in the United States). But the discussions are almost desultory compared to the determination to expand refinery capacity in the Eastern Hemisphere. If the Middle East is gearing up its refinery capacity both locally and by becoming involved with refinery projects in Asia, where are the refined products going to come from in the years that it will take to significantly build new refining capacity in the Western Hemisphere? It looks to us that some large product carriers are going to be awfully busy moving cargoes between the Middle East and the United States in the coming years.
